title: the string too tight snaps, too loose won't play
hookLine: the string too tight snaps, too loose won't play
last: EQUANIMITY — LET IT BE AS IT IS.

cards: There's a monk named Sona, and he is trying so hard. He's been pacing up and down his walking path in meditation so intensely and for so long that his feet are bleeding. The path is stained with it.
And he's getting nowhere. Sitting alone, he starts to think about quitting. Going home.
Using his family's money to do some good in the world instead. The Buddha, the sutta says, knows his thought and comes to him. And he doesn't say try harder.
He doesn't say give up. He asks about music.

teach.b: Before he was a monk, Sona was skilled at the lute, a stringed instrument. So the Buddha asks him: when the strings were too tight, did the lute play well? No.
When the strings were too loose, did it play well? No. And when they were neither too tight nor too loose, but tuned just right?
It's the same with effort, the Buddha says. Too much, and you become restless and strained. Too little, and you become lazy.
Find the right tuning. Sona takes the advice, and the story says that before long, he reaches awakening. This is the middle way, and it's where the Buddha's whole teaching began.
In the first sermon at the deer park, before he taught the four truths, he told his five companions there are two extremes to avoid. On one side, chasing pleasure: the life he'd had in the palace.

On the other, punishing the body: the harsh fasting he'd tried as a seeker. Both, he said, lead nowhere good. Between them runs a middle way, and that middle way is the eightfold path you already know.
So the middle way isn't a bland compromise, halfway between two things. It's more like tuning. A string that's in tune isn't half-tight.
It's exactly right for that string, that instrument, that day.
And it needs retuning, again and again, because strings drift. Some days need more effort. Some days need rest.
The skill isn't finding the answer once. It's listening, and adjusting.

how: Buddhists speak of the middle way as the path between sensual indulgence and self-mortification, and apply it to everyday practice, balancing effort and ease in meditation, eating, sleep and work.

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.
p: tried so hard his feet bled

s: the middle way means a bland compromise
it's like tuning a string: exactly right, and retuned as it drifts.
the Buddha taught the middle way in his first sermon
two extremes to avoid, then the path between them.
the Buddha told Sona to try harder
he asked about the lute: too tight won't play either.

games.q: you're Sona. your feet are bleeding from practice and you're thinking of quitting. the Buddha comes to you. what does he do?
o: tells you to push through the pain.
asks how a lute plays when its strings are too tight.
games.why: he asks about the lute. too tight, too loose: neither plays. effort needs tuning too, and Sona, the story says, soon awakens.

practice: The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Sit, and check your tuning. Is your body too tight?
Clenched jaw, raised shoulders, gripping hands? Let a little go. Is it too loose?
Slumped, drowsy, drifting? Lift the chest a little and brighten your attention. Look for the place in between: upright and relaxed, awake and easy.
When you drift one way or the other, gently retune.

wordCard.voice: The middle way. Between indulgence and self-punishment, not a compromise but a tuning, adjusted again and again. Twentieth word.

orig.note: Pali: the middle way. majjhima, middle; paṭipadā, path, way of practice.

carryVoice: Your line: tune. Not halfway between two things; exactly right for today. That's day twenty.

sources.ref: Sona Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 6.55); also Vinaya, Mahavagga V
